what_its_for: Iron sucrose is used to treat low iron levels (iron deficiency anemia) in people with chronic kidney disease, including those on dialysis or not yet on dialysis. Iron is a mineral your body needs to make healthy red blood cells that carry oxygen throughout your body.
how_to_take: Iron sucrose is given as an injection directly into your vein (intravenous or IV). A nurse or healthcare provider will give you this medicine at a clinic, dialysis center, or hospital. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Each treatment is given slowly over several minutes to hours. You will be watched for any reactions during and after each dose.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose and how often you need treatment based on your kidney condition, your iron levels from blood tests, and your weight. Common schedules include getting a dose 3 times per week during dialysis sessions, or as separate clinic visits if you are not on dialysis. A typical course may be 5 to 10 doses spread over several weeks. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: Since this medicine is given to you by a healthcare provider, contact your doctor or clinic right away if you miss or need to reschedule an appointment. Try not to skip doses, as this can slow your recovery. Your doctor will help you get back on schedule.
storage: Iron sucrose is stored and handled by your healthcare team at the clinic or hospital. You do not need to store this medicine at home. If you are ever given any supplies to take home, keep them at room temperature (59°F to 86°F / 15°C to 30°C), away from light, and out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Tell your healthcare team about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, especially other iron supplements (pills or IV iron), since using more than one iron product at the same time can cause iron overload. Avoid starting new medicines without telling your doctor. Do not take extra iron pills while receiving iron sucrose injections unless your doctor tells you to.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: trouble breathing or shortness of breath, dizziness or feeling faint, rapid or irregular heartbeat, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat, chest pain or tightness, severe rash or itching, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, or low blood pressure. Also call your doctor if you notice: unusual tiredness that is not getting better, pain or swelling at the injection site, signs of too much iron such as joint pain, fatigue, or skin darkening.
when_it_works: You may start to feel more energy and less fatigue within 1 to 4 weeks after starting treatment. However, your blood test results (such as hemoglobin and iron levels) may take several weeks to fully improve. Your doctor will check your blood regularly to track your progress and decide if you need more doses.
special_populations: Older adults: Iron sucrose can be used safely in older patients, but your doctor will monitor you carefully for side effects. Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Iron sucrose is sometimes used during pregnancy when the benefits outweigh the risks, but only under close medical supervision, especially during the first trimester. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of iron may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while receiving this medicine. Children: Iron sucrose can be used in children with chronic kidney disease. The dose is based on the child's weight and will be calculated by the doctor. Kidney disease: This medicine is specifically designed for people with kidney disease, so no special dose adjustment is needed for kidney problems alone.
